passage: I'm Ganga. I sit two desks from Salma at the accounts office, and I've watched her do something I didn't know was possible. When Mohan said he was leaving early for physio, Salma said, just as easily, "I'm off at five too, therapy day." No drama. When Hemant pushed, "Therapy for what?", she smiled and said, "That's mine to keep, but it helps." I think it cost her something, though I can't be sure. Last month our new trainee, Varsha, cried in the washroom after a bad review. Salma didn't say "poor thing". She sat down beside her and said, "Rough day. Want some water? If it keeps feeling heavy, our company counsellor is good." Since then, two people have mentioned their own counselling at lunch as if it were a dentist visit. I don't know if Salma planned that. I just know the room feels different.

qa.q: What did Salma say when Hemant asked "Therapy for what?"
qa.a: That's mine to keep, but it helps.

qa.q: What does Ganga think about how Salma felt when speaking openly?
qa.a: Ganga thinks it may have cost Salma some nerve or discomfort, though Ganga can't be sure.

qa.q: Which choices in the washroom supported Varsha without pity?
qa.a: Salma sat beside her, called it a rough day, offered water and mentioned the company counsellor, without saying "poor thing".

qa.q: Why might Varsha remember Salma's response differently from a "poor thing"?
qa.a: A "poor thing" might have made Varsha feel pitied and small; Salma's calm, ordinary words let it feel like a normal rough day with help available.

grounding: It shows a young woman at work who speaks of therapy as plainly as physio, keeps details private, supports a trainee without pity, and makes it easier for others to talk.

passage:
Diwali, Saturday. At Masi's house, Leela's cousin Sudha barely touched the sweets and said, "I don't know what's wrong with me. I just can't feel anything lately." Leela almost mentioned her own year of therapy, then held back. Too many aunts nearby, and she wasn't ready to say it in a crowd.
The next Thursday. Leela took Sudha for a walk by the lake. "Two years ago I had a really dark stretch," she said. "I saw a psychologist for eight months, the same way I saw a physio after I broke my ankle. It helped." She didn't say "poor you". She asked, "Do you want the name of someone good?"
Three weeks later. A message from Sudha: "Went for my second session. Also told my roommate. She said she's been wanting to go too. Thanks for saying it out loud, Leela."

qa.q: Where did Leela take Sudha the next Thursday?
qa.a: For a walk by the lake.

qa.q: Why did Leela hold back at Masi's house?
qa.a: Too many aunts were nearby, and she felt uneasy and not ready to say it in a crowd.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make on the walk, and why did it work?
qa.a: She shared her own therapy plainly, like physio for an ankle, and offered a name instead of pity, which made help feel normal.

qa.q: How has Leela's openness reached Sudha's roommate?
qa.a: Hearing Sudha talk about it, the roommate admitted wanting to go too, so one honest talk made it easier for the next person.

grounding: It shows a young woman sharing her own therapy only when comfortable, treating it like physical care, supporting her cousin without pity, and the openness spreading.
